templates.name: Main idea, informational study report (incl. explainer and scholar-argument passages)

items.passage: When jellyfish die en masse, their carcasses can sink to the deep seafloor as so-called jelly falls. Because researchers encountering such remains seldom observed scavengers feeding on them, they inferred that gelatinous carcasses transfer comparatively little energy to deep-sea food webs, unlike the carcasses of fish or whales. In baited-camera experiments in Norwegian waters, however, Andrew K. Sweetman et al. recorded more than a thousand hagfish, crabs, shrimp, and amphipods aggregating around jellyfish carcasses and consuming them entirely within roughly two and a half hours, a rate statistically indistinguishable from that for fish carcasses of similar mass.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the earlier observations of jelly falls?
options: They were likely made at depths too great for the hagfish, crabs, and other scavengers that gathered at the baits in Norwegian waters to reach.
They likely involved jellyfish that had sunk more slowly than fish carcasses do and had therefore largely decayed before reaching the seafloor.
They likely gave researchers a misleading impression of how readily deep-sea animals will feed on the remains of jellyfish.
They likely understated how quickly jellyfish carcasses sink, since the remains in the experiments reached the seafloor in roughly two and a half hours.
items.explanation: Earlier researchers “seldom observed scavengers feeding on” jelly falls and inferred that such carcasses “transfer comparatively little energy to deep-sea food webs.” Yet when Sweetman et al. offered jellyfish as bait, more than a thousand scavengers gathered and ate whole carcasses “within roughly two and a half hours,” at a rate “statistically indistinguishable” from that for fish. So the earlier sightings likely gave a misleading picture of how readily deep-sea animals eat jellyfish remains.

A.recipe: plausible but unsupported (invented explanation for the gap)
A.why_wrong: The text never says where or at what depth the earlier observations were made, or that the scavengers in the experiments are absent elsewhere.

B.recipe: plausible but unsupported (invented mechanism, comparison with fish)
B.why_wrong: The text compares how fast scavengers ate jellyfish and fish carcasses, not how fast either sinks, and the earlier observers did find jellyfish remains on the seafloor.

D.recipe: twisted detail (consumption time read as sinking time)
D.why_wrong: Roughly two and a half hours is how long scavengers took to eat the baits, not how long the carcasses took to sink.

sources.what: Sweetman, Smith, Dale and Jones 2014, Proc. R. Soc. B: earlier seafloor observations of jellyfish carcasses lacked the dense scavenger aggregations and rapid consumption typical for vertebrate carrion, leading to a paradigm of limited energy transfer at jelly falls; baited cameras in the Norwegian deep sea drew over 1000 scavengers (Atlantic hagfish, galatheid crabs, decapod shrimp, lysianassid amphipods) that consumed entire jellyfish carcasses in 2.5 h, at rates not significantly different from fish carrion of similar mass

items.notes: Natural science (deep-sea ecology). Chain: the old view rested on seeing few feeders at the remains; the experiments show scavengers eat jellyfish fast and readily; so the old sightings misled. Every option opens on a passage fact; A, B and D each add a link the text never draws. Key paraphrased (misleading impression, readily feed) away from the passage. Band 6.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: PubMed abstract 25320167 (Sweetman et al. 2014): earlier jelly falls showed no dense scavenger aggregations, a paradigm of limited energy transfer; Norwegian baited cameras drew 1000+ scavengers that ate whole carcasses in 2.5 h, rates not different from fish. Key glimpsed while printing the schema before the blind solve; own solve reached C independently.

band7.why: Two linked statements (the old inference rested on few sightings of feeders; baits drew over a thousand at fish-like rates) to an unstated verdict on the old sightings; key paraphrased (misleading impression, readily feed) and the shortest option. A offers an alternative explanation (depth), B an invented sinking mechanism built on the fish comparison, D reads the eating time as sinking time. CID hard cells are planned as band 6 (WAVE.md); a strong band 6.

items.passage: Georgia O’Keeffe noticed tiny blisters forming on the surfaces of some of her oil paintings, and conservators and scholars long assumed that these pin-sized protrusions were grains of sand embedded in the paint. Materials scientist Marc Walton and colleagues, collaborating with the Georgia O’Keeffe Museum, have since identified them as metal soaps, which form when fatty acids in the paint’s binding medium react with lead and zinc pigments and then aggregate, pushing up the paint surface. Notably, on some of the most severely damaged paintings, which conservators had already restored, the protrusions have continued to reappear.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the conservators’ restoration of the damaged paintings?
options: It likely dealt with the bumps that had already formed without halting the chemical reaction within the paint that produces them.
It likely removed most of the sand embedded in the paint, leaving behind only the metal soaps that later spread.
It likely introduced lead and zinc into the paint, supplying the metals from which the later protrusions formed.
It likely showed conservators that the protrusions were metal soaps, not the grains of sand that they and scholars had long taken them to be.
items.explanation: The bumps are “metal soaps” that form when fatty acids in the binding medium “react with lead and zinc pigments,” so their source lies within the paint itself. Some of the most damaged paintings had been restored, yet “the protrusions have continued to reappear.” Together these suggest the restoration treated existing bumps but did not stop the reaction that makes new ones.

B.recipe: twisted detail (the rejected sand explanation treated as fact)
B.why_wrong: The sand explanation is the view the researchers overturned: the bumps were metal soaps, not sand, so there is no sign the restoration removed any sand.

C.recipe: twisted cause (source of the metals moved to the conservators)
C.why_wrong: The lead and zinc come from the paint’s own pigments, which react with the binder; nothing suggests the restoration added these metals.

D.recipe: wrong attribution (the researchers’ finding credited to the restoration)
D.why_wrong: The text credits Walton and colleagues with identifying the metal soaps; it never says the restoration revealed anything about what the protrusions were.

sources.what: Northwestern University news, Feb 2019: O’Keeffe noticed the pin-sized blisters; conservationists and scholars assumed the protrusions were grains of sand; Marc Walton (co-lead) and the Georgia O’Keeffe Museum identified them as metal soaps, free fatty acids in the binding media reacting with lead and zinc pigments, aggregating and pushing the surface up; after conservators restored the most damaged paintings, the protrusions continue to return

items.notes: Arts and science (conservation chemistry). Fame weighed: O’Keeffe is famous, but the item is about the metal-soap finding and the returning protrusions; no background knowledge of her helps. Chain: the soaps come from a reaction inside the paint; restored paintings got the bumps back; so the restoration did not stop the reaction. The smartphone imaging tool and travel effect left out. Band 6.

fixes: last sentence softened to “some of the most severely damaged paintings” (the source says conservators restored some of the most damaged ones) and the stem matched to it
D rebuilt as a wrong attribution (the metal-soap finding credited to the restoration); it was an invented harm comparison, the easiest option, and the key is no longer the longest
review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: Northwestern news, Feb 2019: O’Keeffe noticed the blisters; for decades taken for sand; Walton’s team with the O’Keeffe Museum identified metal soaps (fatty acids reacting with lead and zinc pigments); restored paintings get the protrusions back. Fame call: kept. O’Keeffe is famous, but the tested chain (soaps form inside the paint; restored paintings get them back; so the restoration did not stop the reaction) is not background knowledge, and her fame points to no option.

band7.why: Key needs two premises in different sentences (the soaps come from a reaction within the paint; the bumps return after restoration). B uses the discredited sand view, C moves the metals’ source to the conservators with passage nouns, D credits the restoration with the researchers’ finding. CID hard cells are planned as band 6 (WAVE.md); a strong band 6.

items.passage: Unlike fungi that disperse their spores through the air, truffle-forming fungi produce their fruiting bodies underground and therefore depend on the animals that consume them for dispersal. Many such fungi in Patagonia are mycorrhizal, supplying nutrients to the roots of the Nothofagaceae trees that dominate the region’s forests in exchange for sugars. Although the role of mammals in dispersing these fungi is well documented, Marcos V. Caiafa et al. determined that two common Patagonian birds, the chucao tapaculo and the black-throated huet-huet, routinely consume a diverse array of truffles and excrete viable spores.
items.stem: Based on the text, what role do chucao tapaculos and black-throated huet-huets most likely have in Patagonian forests?
options: They likely compete with mammals for truffles, reducing the number of fungal spores that mammals are able to carry through the forests.
They likely spread the seeds of Nothofagaceae trees, which can then sprout wherever the birds have also deposited truffle spores.
They likely take in from truffles the nutrients that Nothofagaceae trees would otherwise absorb from the soil through their roots.
They likely benefit the forests’ dominant trees by carrying to new sites the fungi that help those trees obtain nourishment.
items.explanation: Truffle fungi “depend on the animals that consume them for dispersal,” and many of them supply “nutrients to the roots of the Nothofagaceae trees that dominate the region’s forests.” The two birds “routinely consume a diverse array of truffles and excrete viable spores.” So by spreading these fungi, the birds most likely help the forests’ main trees indirectly.

A.why_wrong: Mammals are said to disperse these fungi too, but the text never suggests the birds reduce what mammals eat or spread.

B.why_wrong: The birds excrete fungal spores, not tree seeds; the text says nothing about the birds eating or spreading the seeds of Nothofagaceae trees.

C.why_wrong: The fungi supply nutrients to the trees in exchange for sugars; nothing suggests that the birds’ eating truffles deprives the trees of nutrients from the soil.

sources.what: Caiafa, Jusino, Wilkie, Díaz, Sieving and Smith 2021, Current Biology: truffle fungi rely on animals for spore dispersal; the role of mammals is well documented but birds understudied; chucao tapaculos and black-throated huet-huets regularly consume mycorrhizal fungi, including many truffles associated with the Nothofagaceae trees that dominate Patagonian forests, and disperse viable spores (metagenomics and epifluorescence microscopy of feces); mycorrhizal fungi feed nutrients to plants in exchange for sugars

items.notes: Natural science (ecology, Chile). Chain: truffles need animals to spread; the fungi feed the dominant trees; the birds spread viable spores; so the birds likely help the trees indirectly. Different logic from w5b1_01 (that one turned on a sole disperser and nurse shrubs). Key hedged with likely, as are all options. Band 6.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: PubMed abstract 34715015 (Caiafa et al. 2021): chucao tapaculos and black-throated huet-huets routinely eat truffles and other mycorrhizal fungi of the Nothofagaceae and disperse viable spores; mycorrhizal fungi feed nutrients to plants for sugars. Concept overlap noted: live w5b1_01 also has an animal disperser that helps plants indirectly (a lizard, seeds, nurse plants); spores rather than seeds and the mycorrhizal link make it a different item, kept.

band7.why: Key chains three statements (truffles need animals to spread; the fungi feed the dominant trees; the birds excrete viable spores) to an unstated benefit to the trees. B twists spores into seeds, C turns eating truffles into taking the trees’ nutrients, A invents competition with mammals. CID hard cells are planned as band 6 (WAVE.md); a strong band 6.

items.passage: Reconstructing variations in the intensity of Earth’s magnetic field before the advent of modern instruments relies on ancient materials such as fired clay and poses two challenges: estimating the past field accurately and dating the materials precisely. Erez Ben-Yosef et al. addressed the latter using storage jar handles from ancient Judah bearing royal stamp impressions whose designs changed with the political powers governing the region, enabling each jar’s firing to be closely dated. Their record of the eighth to second centuries BCE supports earlier evidence of a brief spike in field intensity in the late eighth century BCE.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: By developing a more accurate way to measure the field recorded in fired clay, researchers have shown that the field remained essentially stable from the eighth to the second centuries BCE.
Because stamps on Judean jar handles reveal when the jars were fired, researchers could build a precisely dated record of field strength that adds weight to earlier signs of a short-lived surge.
Shifts in the intensity of Earth’s magnetic field recorded in fired clay have allowed researchers to determine when different political powers ruled ancient Judah.
Royal stamp impressions from ancient Judah measure the past strength of Earth’s magnetic field more accurately than other kinds of fired clay can.
items.explanation: The text names two challenges, “estimating the past field accurately and dating the materials precisely,” and says Ben-Yosef et al. “addressed the latter”: the stamps’ designs “changed with the political powers governing the region,” so “each jar’s firing” could be “closely dated.” The resulting record “supports earlier evidence of a brief spike.” Choice B joins both steps.

A.why_wrong: The team addressed dating, not measurement accuracy, and its record supports a brief spike rather than a stable field.

C.why_wrong: The stamps, which reflect the political powers, were used to date the jars; the magnetic record was not used to date the rulers.

D.why_wrong: The stamps help with dating; the text never says they measure the field more accurately than other fired clay.

sources.what: Ben-Yosef, Millman, Shaar, Tauxe and Lipschits 2017, PNAS: reconstructing past geomagnetic field behavior has twin challenges of accuracy of paleomagnetic estimates and dating of the archaeological material; royal Judean stamped storage jar handles address the latter because stamp typology corresponds to changes in the ruling political entities; record of the eighth to second centuries BCE gives further support for a short interval of extreme high values in the late eighth century BCE

items.notes: Archaeology and geophysics. Spread main idea: the method (stamps date the firing) and the result (support for a spike) sit in different sentences; the key must carry both. Distractors: wrong challenge plus contradicted result, reversed direction, invented comparison. Band 6.

fixes: key paraphrased away from the passage (“closely dated”, “supports earlier evidence of a brief spike” became “precisely dated”, “adds weight to earlier signs of a short-lived surge”)
A trimmed by one word (“the magnetic field” to “the field”) to keep the batch key-longest rate in check_rw’s range
review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: PubMed abstract 28193874 (Ben-Yosef et al. 2017, PNAS): twin challenges of accuracy and dating; stamp typology tracks the ruling powers and dates the firing; record of the 8th to 2nd centuries BCE supports a short spike in the late 8th century BCE.

band7.why: Main idea spread over the method and the result in different sentences; A takes the other challenge and contradicts the spike, C reverses what dates what, D invents an accuracy comparison. CID hard cells are planned as band 6 (WAVE.md); a strong band 6.

items.passage: Among birds, the ability to learn vocalizations by imitation is thought to have evolved in only three groups (parrots, hummingbirds, and oscine songbirds), while suboscines, a related group of perching birds, are generally held to inherit their songs. Behavioral observations had suggested that the three-wattled bellbird, a Central American suboscine, might be an exception: its populations sing strikingly different songs that also change over time. Comparing the birds’ DNA with their songs, Vinodkumar Saranathan et al. found that populations singing different songs were only weakly differentiated genetically, which the team took as support for an independent origin of vocal learning in the bellbird.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Although suboscine birds are generally believed to be born knowing their songs, genetic evidence suggests that the three-wattled bellbird acquires its songs by learning them.
Genetic evidence indicates that the bellbird populations that sing different songs are in fact separate species, which would explain why each population sings its own distinctive song.
Bellbird songs change too rapidly over time for researchers to determine whether the differences among the birds’ songs have a genetic basis.
The bellbird’s ability to learn its songs suggests that vocal learning arose only once among birds, in an ancestor shared by parrots, hummingbirds, oscines, and suboscines.
items.explanation: Suboscines “are generally held to inherit their songs,” but bellbird populations “sing strikingly different songs.” Saranathan et al. found these populations “only weakly differentiated genetically,” so the song differences are unlikely to be inherited, which the team “took as support for an independent origin of vocal learning in the bellbird.” Choice A holds both the usual view and the revision.

B.why_wrong: The populations with different songs were “only weakly differentiated genetically,” the opposite of being separate species.

C.why_wrong: The songs do change over time, but the researchers did reach a conclusion by comparing DNA with songs.

D.recipe: twisted detail (independent origin read as a single shared origin)
D.why_wrong: The team saw support for an “independent origin” of vocal learning in the bellbird, not a single origin in a shared ancestor.

sources.what: Saranathan, Hamilton, Powell, Kroodsma and Prum 2007, Molecular Ecology: vocal learning thought to have evolved in parrots, hummingbirds and oscine passerines; behavioural data indicate that, unlike other suboscines, the three-wattled bellbird can learn songs, with striking geographical variation and rapid temporal change; mtDNA and microsatellites show vocally differentiated populations only weakly genetically differentiated; data support a fourth, independent origin of avian vocal learning in Procnias; dialects likely culturally evolved

items.notes: Natural science (animal behavior, Costa Rica and Central America). View then correction: suboscines inherit songs; bellbird genetics do not track song, so songs are likely learned. Key hedged as the abstract is (supports the view). Band 6.

fixes: key paraphrased away from the passage (inherit, a genetic comparison supports the view) as “born knowing their songs”, “genetic evidence suggests”
review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: PubMed abstract 17845441 (Saranathan et al. 2007): vocal learning in three avian clades; bellbird populations with different songs only weakly differentiated genetically; support for a fourth, independent origin of vocal learning.

band7.why: View then correction with a two-part key. B and D each fall to one stated fact (weak differentiation; independent origin), but both open on a true clause (genetic evidence about the populations; the bellbird learns its songs) and fail on a later link; C misuses the true detail that songs change. Acceptable band 6, not rebuilt. CID hard cells are planned as band 6 (WAVE.md); a strong band 6.

items.passage: Richard Ligon’s 1657 account of early colonial Barbados, accompanied by a celebrated map, has traditionally been interpreted as documenting the introduction of Old World animals after European contact, including pigs supposedly released by passing sailors during the previous century. Christina M. Giovas et al., however, identified a jawbone from a historic archaeological deposit on the island as belonging to a peccary, a piglike mammal of the Americas frequently mistaken for the wild boar. Isotopic analysis indicated that the animal had lived on Barbados, and the researchers argue that some of Ligon’s “pigs” were likely peccaries, probably introduced from northern South America.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Archaeological evidence confirms Ligon’s report that passing sailors released European pigs on Barbados about a century before English settlement began.
Although Ligon described European pigs on early colonial Barbados, new evidence shows that every animal he called a pig was in fact a peccary brought from South America.
Isotopic analysis shows that peccaries reached Barbados before any Old World animals did, overturning the long-held view that no large mammals lived on the island before European contact.
Although Ligon’s account has long been read as recording European pigs on Barbados, new evidence suggests that the animals he called pigs included a piglike mammal from the Americas.
items.explanation: Ligon’s account “has traditionally been interpreted as documenting the introduction of Old World animals,” including pigs. But Giovas et al. identified a peccary jawbone from an animal that “had lived on Barbados,” and they argue that some of Ligon’s “pigs” “were likely peccaries.” Choice D states the earlier reading and the revision, with “a piglike mammal from the Americas” standing for the peccary.

A.why_wrong: The evidence challenges, rather than confirms, the reading of Ligon’s “pigs” as European animals released by sailors.

B.recipe: overstated degree (some read as all) in the key’s frame
B.why_wrong: The researchers argue only that some of Ligon’s “pigs” “were likely peccaries,” not that every one was; the text does not rule out European pigs on the island as well.

C.why_wrong: The text does not say peccaries arrived before every Old World animal, and it never mentions a view that Barbados had no large mammals before contact.

sources.what: Giovas, Kamenov and Krigbaum 2019, PLoS ONE: Richard Ligon’s 17th-century account and celebrated map of colonial Barbados records Old World species, including pigs believed released by passing sailors the century prior; a securely identified peccary mandible from a historic archaeological context; 87Sr/86Sr and AMS radiocarbon indicate local origin; ‘pigs’ were in fact peccaries, a New World mammal often confused with wild boars, most likely introduced in the 16th century from the Guianas/Trinidad

items.notes: History and archaeology (Caribbean). View then correction with the source’s hedges kept (likely, probably). Wording ‘South American mainland region’ stands for the Guianas/Trinidad. Band 6.

fixes: key paraphrased away from the passage (“some of his ‘pigs’ were peccaries” became “the animals he called pigs included a piglike mammal from the Americas”)
B rebuilt in the key’s Although frame as a degree trap (every “pig” a peccary, against the passage’s some); it was an overstated historians’ verdict
C lengthened so the key is not the longest option
review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: PubMed abstract 31086373 (Giovas, Kamenov, Krigbaum 2019): Ligon’s 1657 account and map long read as recording Old World pigs released by sailors; peccary mandible of local origin by strontium isotopes; Ligon’s “pigs” peccaries, most likely brought from the Guianas or Trinidad; the map shows both peccary and domestic swine.

band7.why: Key must keep the passage’s degree (some, not all) and the earlier reading; B now shares the frame and fails only on degree, A confirms what the evidence challenges, C invents a priority claim. CID hard cells are planned as band 6 (WAVE.md); a strong band 6.

items.passage:
The following text is Ralph Hodgson’s 1913 poem “Stupidity Street.” Hodgson was an English poet, and many of his poems concern birds and other animals.

I saw with open eyes
Singing birds sweet
Sold in the shops
For the people to eat,
Sold in the shops of
Stupidity Street.

I saw in vision
The worm in the wheat,
And in the shops nothing
For people to eat;
Nothing for sale in
Stupidity Street.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Wheat and bread will one day replace the songbirds now sold as food in the shops on Stupidity Street.
The speaker is saddened that the people who buy songbirds in the shops cannot afford to buy any other kind of food.
Killing songbirds for food may leave people hungry, since without the birds pests could ruin the crops.
The speaker warns that a disease spreading through the wheat fields will soon force the shops to sell songbirds as food.
items.explanation: The first stanza shows “Singing birds sweet” being “Sold in the shops / For the people to eat.” The second imagines what follows: “The worm in the wheat” and “in the shops nothing / For people to eat.” With the birds that eat such worms gone, pests ruin the grain, which is why the street is named for stupidity. Choice C states that point.

A.why_wrong: The vision is of empty shops, “nothing / For people to eat,” not of shops selling wheat or bread in place of songbirds.

B.why_wrong: The poem says nothing about what people can afford; it blames the selling of songbirds, not poverty.

D.why_wrong: The songbirds are already being sold in the first stanza; the worm in the wheat is the later result, not the cause.

sources.what: text of “Stupidity Street” (The Year’s at the Spring, 1920, Wikisource)
first publication in Hodgson’s The Mystery and Other Poems (Flying Fame, 1913); contents of Poems (1917) list The Birdcatcher, The Swallow, The Bull, The Late, Last Rook

items.notes: Literature (poem, public domain, whole poem copied exactly; small-capital ‘I SAW’ set as ‘I saw’). Hard because the key rests on an unstated link (birds keep the worm out of the wheat). The 1920 anthology’s editor reads it the same way: it does not say killing birds is wrong, it names a street and gives a reason. Context line added to reach the models’ length and checked against Hodgson’s contents (bird poems). Band 6.

fixes: A rewritten without the “The speaker” opening, so the key is no longer the only option in a different frame (now two and two)
review.facts_note: Text checked against Wikisource (The Year’s at the Spring, 1920) and the 1913 Flying Fame chapbook The Mystery and Other Poems on archive.org: exact, first published 1913.

band7.why: Key rests on an unstated link (songbirds keep the worm out of the wheat) and the stance of the street’s name; D reverses cause and effect with the poem’s own nouns, A reads the vision as hopeful, B invents poverty. CID hard cells are planned as band 6 (WAVE.md); a strong band 6.

items.passage: When English-speaking preschoolers see a hand holding up fingers to represent a number, they tend to interpret the gesture as a single shape standing for that number rather than counting the raised fingers individually. Psychologist Elena Nicoladis and her colleagues wondered whether children learn to associate each finger with one unit by encountering several different finger patterns for the same quantity. They therefore compared English-speaking children with children who also spoke French or German and had consequently been exposed to more than one such pattern. As predicted, the bilingual children were more successful at interpreting unfamiliar number gestures.
items.stem: According to the text, why did the researchers compare English-speaking children with children who also spoke French or German?
options: They expected the bilingual children to have learned to read number gestures as single shapes at a younger age.
They wanted to see whether seeing several finger patterns for one number helps children learn to count fingers individually.
They suspected that the bilingual children counted aloud more often than the English-speaking children did.
They hoped to learn whether children who speak two languages use number gestures more often when they talk.
items.explanation: The researchers “wondered whether children learn to associate each finger with one unit by encountering several different finger patterns for the same quantity,” and the French- or German-speaking children “had consequently been exposed to more than one such pattern.” Comparing the two groups tested that idea, as choice B says.

A.recipe: twisted detail (the habit the text attributes to English-speaking preschoolers)
A.why_wrong: Reading a gesture as “a single shape” is what English-speaking preschoolers tend to do; the comparison was about learning to count fingers, not about doing that earlier.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how often any of the children counted aloud.

D.why_wrong: The study concerned interpreting number gestures, not how often children use gestures while talking.

sources.what: Nicoladis, Marentette and Pika 2019, Developmental Science: monolingual English-speaking preschoolers process number gestures as unanalyzed wholes rather than one-to-one; study tested whether exposure to a variety of finger configurations for one quantity teaches one-to-one correspondence; French-English and German-English bilinguals (exposure to multiple configurations) vs English monolinguals; as predicted, bilinguals better at interpreting unconventional number gestures

items.notes: Social science (developmental psychology). Framed as exposure to several counting patterns, not as a general bilingual advantage (that frame is a live Cross-Text item). Study 2 (Chinese-English children) left out.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: PubMed abstract 30516316 (Nicoladis, Marentette, Pika 2019): test of whether exposure to several finger configurations for one quantity teaches one-to-one correspondence; French-English and German-English bilinguals better, as predicted.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Netta Syrett’s 1921 novel Rachel and the Seven Wonders. Miss Moore is Rachel’s governess.

Rachel was a very unhappy little girl as she sat in an omnibus with Miss Moore, on her way to the British Museum. She didn’t want to go to the British Museum. She didn’t want to be in London at all. She longed desperately to be back in her country home with her father and mother—now, alas! far away in Egypt.

Aunt Hester, who was her father’s eldest sister, and in the eyes of Rachel, at least, awfully old, was quite kind, but also, as she admitted, quite unused to children. The first thing she did therefore, was to engage a governess to look after her niece for the seven weeks she would have to remain with her.
items.stem: According to the text, why did Aunt Hester hire a governess for Rachel?
options: Rachel’s parents had asked her to find someone to give Rachel lessons while they were away in Egypt.
She wanted someone to take Rachel to the British Museum, a place she herself did not care to visit.
She thought that Rachel was too unhappy in London to be left on her own during the day.
She did not feel prepared to look after a child by herself for several weeks.
items.explanation: Aunt Hester was “quite kind, but also, as she admitted, quite unused to children,” and “the first thing she did therefore, was to engage a governess to look after her niece.” Choice D restates that reason.

A.why_wrong: Rachel’s parents are said to be “far away in Egypt,” but the text never says they asked for a governess or for lessons.

B.why_wrong: The governess does take Rachel to the British Museum, but the text gives no sign that Aunt Hester disliked the place or hired the governess for that trip.

C.recipe: twisted detail (Rachel’s feeling given as the aunt’s reason)
C.why_wrong: Rachel is “very unhappy,” but the text gives Aunt Hester’s unfamiliarity with children, not Rachel’s mood, as the reason for the governess.

sources.what: text of Rachel and the Seven Wonders (original publication 1921; US edition Frederick A. Stokes 1923), First Wonder

items.notes: Literature (English children’s novel, 1921, public domain in the US). Copied exactly; the paragraph between the two used here (why Rachel was sent to London) is cut at the paragraph boundary. Replaces Explorers of the Dawn, which b2 claimed first.

review.facts_note: Excerpt checked against Gutenberg #66321 (original publication 1921): exact, one paragraph cut at its boundary.

items.passage: Ticks that feed on three different hosts during their lives typically detach from each host after a blood meal and molt into their next developmental stage on the ground. Parasitologist Sándor Hornok and colleagues, however, discovered that roughly one in five of the more than 3,000 immature ticks they collected from insectivorous songbirds had already begun molting while still attached to the birds. The researchers linked this phenomenon to ecdysteroids, hormones that regulate molting in insects and ticks: several of the birds’ blood samples contained these compounds, which the birds likely acquired from the caterpillars they consumed.
items.stem: According to the text, what was unusual about some of the ticks that the researchers collected?
options: They had started to molt before dropping off the birds they were feeding on.
They had fed on several different songbird species before they were collected.
They contained more ecdysteroids than the caterpillars eaten by the birds did.
They had skipped one of the life stages that such ticks normally pass through.
items.explanation: Such ticks normally “detach from each host after a blood meal and molt” on the ground, but about one in five of the ticks collected “had already begun molting while still attached to the birds.” Choice A states this.

B.why_wrong: The text says these ticks feed on three hosts over their lives, not that the collected ticks had fed on several songbird species.

C.why_wrong: Ecdysteroids were found in the birds’ blood; the text never measures them in the ticks or compares any amounts with the caterpillars’.

D.why_wrong: The ticks began molting early, in an unusual place; nothing suggests they skipped a life stage.

sources.what: Hornok et al. 2016, Scientific Reports: three-host ixodid ticks normally moult off-host after the blood meal; 3330 tick larvae and nymphs from 1164 insectivorous songbirds of 46 species; 20.5% showed apolysis (first step of moulting) on the birds, correlated with seasonality of lepidopteran caterpillars; 8 of 18 bird blood samples contained ecdysteroids, associated with tick apolysis

items.notes: Natural science (parasitology). ‘Begun to molt’ stands for apolysis, the first step of molting. Collection site not named (the abstract does not give it).

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: PubMed abstract 26996354 (Hornok et al. 2016): 20.5% of 3,330 tick larvae and nymphs on songbirds began moulting on the host; ecdysteroids in 8 of 18 bird blood samples, linked to caterpillar season.

items.passage: Stars passing near the solar system can disturb the Oort Cloud, a vast shell of icy bodies surrounding the Sun, potentially sending comets toward the inner planets. Using velocity measurements of Scholz’s star, a small, recently discovered binary system, astronomer Eric Mamajek and colleagues reconstructed its past trajectory and determined that approximately 70,000 years ago it passed through the outer Oort Cloud, the closest well-measured stellar flyby known at the time. Because the binary has relatively little mass and was traveling rapidly, however, its passage probably had a negligible effect on comets.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers found that Scholz’s star sent a shower of comets toward the inner planets when it passed near the Sun about 70,000 years ago.
Astronomers discovered Scholz’s star by tracking the effects that its passage had on the orbits of comets in the outer Oort Cloud.
Researchers determined that a small star system passed through the outer Oort Cloud long ago but likely did little to disturb the comets there.
Most stars passing through the Oort Cloud are too small and fast to disturb its comets, so comet showers caused by passing stars are rare.
items.explanation: Mamajek and colleagues determined that Scholz’s star “passed through the outer Oort Cloud” about 70,000 years ago, “the closest well-measured stellar flyby known at the time,” but that because it “has relatively little mass and was traveling rapidly,” its passage “probably had a negligible effect on comets.” Choice C joins the finding and its limit.

A.why_wrong: The passage “probably had a negligible effect on comets,” so it did not send a comet shower inward.

B.why_wrong: The team reconstructed the star’s path from “velocity measurements”; the star was not found through effects on comets.

D.why_wrong: The text explains why this one binary had little effect; it says nothing about most passing stars or how often comet showers occur.

sources.what: Mamajek et al. 2015, ApJ Letters (arXiv 1502.04655): passing stars can perturb the Oort Cloud and trigger comet showers; velocity measurements of the recently discovered low-mass binary Scholz’s star give a past trajectory passing about 52 kAU from the Sun 70 kya, within the outer Oort Cloud; the closest known encounter with well-constrained distance and velocity; low mass and high velocity made the encounter dynamically weak, with likely negligible impact on the flux of long-period comets

items.notes: Natural science (astronomy). Two-part key (finding plus its limit). Exact distance and uncertainties left out.

fixes: “the closest well-measured stellar flyby on record” changed to “known at the time”, as the 2015 paper states it for its date
review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: arXiv 1502.04655 abstract (Mamajek et al. 2015): Scholz’s star passed about 52 kAU from the Sun 70 kya, in the outer Oort Cloud, closest known encounter with well-constrained distance and velocity; low mass and high speed, likely negligible effect on comets.

items.passage: Mathematicians often describe proofs as “beautiful” or “dull,” but do people without mathematical training experience mathematics in a similar way? To find out, psychologist Samuel G. B. Johnson and mathematician Stefan Steinerberger asked participants to rate how similar several simple mathematical arguments were to particular landscape paintings and, in a second study, to pieces of classical piano music. Participants’ judgments were consistent with one another, and when rating beauty in both the arguments and the artworks, they relied mostly on the same qualities, such as elegance and clarity.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Research shows that mathematicians and people without mathematical training tend to disagree about which mathematical arguments are beautiful.
A study suggests that people without mathematical training respond to mathematical ideas aesthetically, much as they respond to art.
A study found that people consider landscape paintings and piano music more beautiful than simple mathematical arguments.
Researchers found that people who enjoy classical piano music are better than others at understanding mathematical arguments.
items.explanation: The researchers asked whether people “without mathematical training experience mathematics in a similar way” to mathematicians. Participants matched arguments to paintings and music consistently and judged beauty in “both the arguments and the artworks” by “the same qualities.” So people without training appear to experience mathematics aesthetically, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: The text reports what untrained participants did; it never compares their judgments with mathematicians’ or reports disagreement.

C.why_wrong: Participants rated similarity and the qualities behind beauty; the text never says they ranked the artworks above the arguments.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text links enjoying piano music to understanding mathematics.

sources.what: Johnson and Steinerberger 2019, Cognition: do laypeople experience mathematics aesthetically; similarity ratings of simple mathematical arguments to landscape paintings (Study 1) and classical piano pieces (Study 2) were internally consistent across participants; beauty judged mainly by elegance, profundity and clarity for both artworks and arguments

items.notes: Social science (psychology of aesthetics). Opens with the study’s own question, as official 2.20 and 3.20 do.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: PubMed abstract 31015078 (Johnson and Steinerberger 2019): laypeople’s similarity ratings of arguments to paintings and piano pieces consistent; beauty judged on the same dimensions (elegance, profundity, clarity).

items.passage: For generations, bait collectors in Florida’s Apalachicola National Forest have gathered earthworms by “grunting”: vibrating a wooden stake driven into the soil, which can bring thousands of worms to the surface within a few hours. Biologist Kenneth Catania found that eastern moles, which hunt earthworms underground, inhabit the area and that the worms rapidly flee across the surface when a mole approaches. His recordings also showed that the vibrations produced by grunters resemble those produced by digging moles.
items.stem: Based on the text, why do the earthworms most likely come to the surface in response to grunting?
options: They react to the vibrations as though a predator were approaching through the soil.
They sense that rain is falling and leave their burrows to avoid drowning.
They are drawn upward by vibrations that resemble the movements of other worms.
They are fleeing moles that the grunters’ vibrations have driven up toward the surface.
items.explanation: The worms “rapidly flee across the surface when a mole approaches,” and the vibrations made by grunters “resemble those produced by digging moles.” Together these suggest that the worms surface because they treat grunting as the approach of a predator, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: Rain is never mentioned; the text links the vibrations to digging moles.

C.why_wrong: The recordings matched grunters’ vibrations to digging moles, not to other worms.

D.why_wrong: The grunters’ vibrations imitate moles; nothing suggests they drive real moles anywhere.

sources.what: Catania 2008, PLoS ONE: worm grunting in and around Apalachicola National Forest, vibrating a wooden stake driven into the soil, thousands of Diplocardia mississippiensis gathered in a few hours; eastern American moles inhabit the area; earthworms have a pronounced escape response from moles, rapidly exiting burrows to flee across the surface; recordings suggest worm grunters unknowingly mimic digging moles; the rain hypothesis is not supported

items.notes: Natural science (animal behavior). Two premises in different sentences (escape from moles; grunting sounds like moles); the conclusion is left unstated. Rain decoy is the study’s rejected alternative, which the passage does not raise.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: PubMed abstract 18852902 (Catania 2008): grunters’ vibrations mimic digging moles; worms flee moles across the surface; rain hypothesis not supported. Catania is also named in a live Words in Context item (star-nosed mole smelling underwater), a different finding: kept.

items.passage: Paraguayan artist Feliciano Centurión (1962–1996), who learned to crochet and sew as a boy from the women of his household, worked mostly with soft household fabrics such as blankets, handkerchiefs, aprons, pillowcases, and tablecloths. In Buenos Aires in the 1990s, he bought inexpensive patterned blankets at local markets and then painted and embroidered them with images of plants and animals, sometimes adding short phrases of a personal, diarylike kind.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Centurión became well known in Paraguay for reviving crochet patterns that had nearly disappeared from use.
Centurión painted on blankets mainly because he could not afford canvas while he was living in Buenos Aires.
Centurión’s work grew more abstract over time as he gradually stopped depicting plants and animals.
Centurión transformed ordinary household textiles into works of art by painting and embroidering on them.
items.explanation: Centurión “worked mostly with soft household fabrics” and “painted and embroidered” cheap market blankets “with images of plants and animals.” Choice D generalizes these examples.

A.why_wrong: He learned to crochet as a boy, but the text says nothing about reviving old patterns or about fame in Paraguay.

B.why_wrong: The blankets were inexpensive, but the text gives no reason for his choice and never mentions canvas.

C.why_wrong: The text describes no change in his style over time; plants and animals appear in the 1990s work it describes.

sources.what: Feliciano Centurión (1962–1996): Paraguayan artist in Buenos Aires; as a child taught to crochet and sew by the women of his household; worked with soft fabrics (blankets, handkerchiefs, aprons, pillowcases, tablecloths); painted and embroidered inexpensive patterned blankets (frazadas) bought at local markets; motifs included diaristic texts and flora and fauna

items.notes: Arts (textile art, Paraguay and Argentina). Profile: medium, examples, effect generalized in the key. His illness and death left out.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: Wikipedia, Feliciano Centurión: taught to crochet and sew by the women of his household; soft fabrics (blankets, handkerchiefs, aprons, pillowcases, tablecloths); painted and embroidered cheap market blankets in Buenos Aires; flora, fauna and diaristic texts.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Jorge Isaacs’s 1867 novel María (translated by Rollo Ogden in 1890). The narrator is returning to his family’s home in Colombia’s Cauca Valley after six years at school in Bogotá.

After six years, the last days of a splendid August saw me returning to my native valley. My heart was overflowing with love of home. It was the last day of my journey, and I was enjoying the most charming morning of the autumn. I was struck dumb by all this beauty, though I thought I had preserved it in my memory, because some verses of mine, admired by my fellow-students, gave faint suggestions of it. So the sky, the horizon, the plains, the crests of Cauca, make those speechless who behold them. The great beauties of nature cannot be sung at the same time they are seen; they must return to the soul, made dim by a faulty memory.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The narrator regrets that the poems he wrote at school exaggerated the beauty of his native valley.
Overwhelmed by the valley’s beauty on his return, the narrator reflects that such scenes can be put into words only later, from memory.
The narrator is disappointed to find that his native valley is less beautiful than he had remembered it.
Back in his native valley, the narrator resolves to write verses about its beauty while the scene is still before his eyes.
items.explanation: The narrator is “struck dumb by all this beauty,” although he thought he had kept it in memory, and he concludes that “the great beauties of nature cannot be sung at the same time they are seen; they must return to the soul.” Choice B states both his reaction and his reflection.

A.why_wrong: His school verses “gave faint suggestions” of the valley’s beauty, so they fell short of it rather than exaggerating it.

C.why_wrong: He is “struck dumb by all this beauty,” the opposite of disappointment.

D.why_wrong: He says such beauty “cannot be sung at the same time” it is seen, so he does not plan to write while looking at it.

sources.what: text of Maria: A South American Romance, translated by Rollo Ogden (Harper and Brothers, 1890), chapter II; chapter I gives the school in Bogotá

items.notes: Literature (Colombian novel in an 1890 translation, public domain). Adapted by cutting two sentences (the plains description and the ballroom simile) at sentence boundaries; OCR line-break hyphens rejoined. The ‘So’ sentence, which compared the landscape with the simile, now follows the narrator’s own speechlessness.

review.facts_note: Excerpt checked against the 1890 Harper edition on archive.org (Ogden translation, chapter II): exact, cuts at sentence boundaries; Bogotá school in chapter I.

items.passage: El Niño events, which bring torrential rains and flooding to the normally arid northern coast of Peru, have often been characterized as disasters that disrupt agriculture, both today and in the region’s past. But archaeologist Ari Caramanica and colleagues have found that in the Pampa de Mocan, a coastal desert plain, prehispanic farmers practiced floodwater farming for some 2,000 years, constructing canal systems that could channel both river water and El Niño floodwaters to their fields. Consequently, the farmers were able to cultivate terrain that would otherwise have been marginal.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Ancient farmers in the Pampa de Mocan abandoned their fields during El Niño years and returned to them once the floods had passed.
Modern flood control projects in northern Peru are based on canal designs that were first developed by prehispanic farmers in the Pampa de Mocan.
Although El Niño floods are usually seen as destructive, prehispanic farmers on Peru’s northern coast built canals to put the floods to use.
Because El Niño events were uncommon in prehispanic times, ancient farmers on Peru’s northern coast seldom had to cope with flooding.
items.explanation: El Niño events “have often been characterized as disasters that disrupt agriculture,” but in the Pampa de Mocan prehispanic farmers constructed “canal systems that could channel both river water and El Niño floodwaters to their fields.” Choice C holds the usual view and the correction.

A.why_wrong: The farmers used El Niño floodwaters on their fields rather than leaving them.

B.why_wrong: The text says nothing about modern flood control borrowing these designs.

D.why_wrong: The text never says how often El Niño events occurred in the past, and the farmers’ canals were built to use their floods.

sources.what: Caramanica et al. 2020, PNAS: El Niño treated as a disruptor in ancient and modern Peru; in the Pampa de Mocan, a coastal desert plain, prehispanic irrigation systems were designed to incorporate floods and convert them into productive waters; a 2,000-year history of floodwater farming embedded in canal systems taking advantage of El Niño floodwaters as well as river water; ancient farmers used floodwaters to develop otherwise marginal landscapes

items.notes: Archaeology (Peru). View then correction; the policy point of the paper left out.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: PubMed abstract 32900937 (Caramanica et al. 2020): El Niño seen as a disruptor; Pampa de Mocan canals took in floodwaters for 2,000 years and made marginal land productive.

items.passage: In the late 1970s, the development organization RDRS sought to create an affordable irrigation pump for impoverished farmers in northern Bangladesh. The organization required that the pump irrigate at least half a hectare of wheat. Its total cost, including installation, could not exceed the price of one bag of rice, and it had to be simple enough to manufacture and repair locally. The result, completed in 1979 by Norwegian designer Gunnar Barnes, was the treadle pump. Powered entirely by a person stepping on foot levers, it requires no fuel.
items.stem: According to the text, what was one requirement that RDRS set for the pump?
options: It had to run on a kind of fuel that farmers could buy cheaply.
It had to be designed by an engineer who lived in Bangladesh.
It had to be simple enough to make and fix in the local area.
It had to be able to water at least one hectare of rice.
items.explanation: Among other requirements, the pump “had to be simple enough to manufacture and repair locally.” Choice C restates this requirement.

A.why_wrong: The treadle pump is “powered entirely by a person stepping on foot levers” and “requires no fuel.”

B.why_wrong: The design is credited to “Norwegian designer Gunnar Barnes,” and the text sets no rule about where the designer lived.

D.why_wrong: The pump had to “irrigate at least half a hectare of wheat”; rice appears only as the measure of its maximum cost.

sources.what: Treadle pump: RDRS (Lutheran World Federation programme) in northern Bangladesh sought a low-cost irrigation pump from 1975; model by Norwegian intermediate technologist Gunnar Barnes developed in 1979; criteria: irrigate at least 0.5 ha of wheat, purchase and installation no more than the price of one bag of paddy, simple enough to make and repair locally; operated by stepping on treadles; needs no fossil fuel

items.notes: Technology (low-cost irrigation, Bangladesh). Paddy rendered as rice. Replaces the kangaroo-care subject, already a live Boundaries item.

fixes: Gunnar Barnes called a designer rather than an engineer (the source calls him an intermediate technologist who developed the model)
review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: Wikipedia, Treadle pump: RDRS criteria (0.5 ha of wheat, cost no more than a bag of paddy, made and repaired locally); model developed by Gunnar Barnes in 1979; needs no fossil fuel.

items.passage: In 2003, Singapore’s national water agency, the Public Utilities Board (PUB), began distributing NEWater, recycled water that has been purified so thoroughly that it is safe to drink. The water is passed through very fine filters and then treated with ultraviolet light. Anticipating that some residents would worry about the safety of recycled water, PUB avoided words such as “sewage” and “wastewater,” calling it “used water” instead, and it renamed sewage treatment plants “water reclamation plants.” It also opened a visitor center where people could see how NEWater is made.
items.stem: According to the text, why did PUB avoid words such as “sewage”?
options: It expected that some people would be concerned about whether recycled water was safe.
It wanted people to know that NEWater was meant mainly for use in factories.
Those words were difficult to translate into the other languages spoken in Singapore.
Visitors to the NEWater center had complained about those words.
items.explanation: PUB avoided such words because it was “anticipating that some residents would worry about the safety of recycled water.” Choice A restates this reason.

B.why_wrong: The text says nothing about factories; it describes NEWater as water “safe to drink.”

D.why_wrong: The visitor center is another step PUB took; the text gives no complaints from visitors.

sources.what: NEWater: PUB launched NEWater to the public in 2003; potable reclaimed water made by microfiltration, reverse osmosis and ultraviolet treatment; anticipating public concerns over safety, PUB avoided terms such as wastewater or sewage, renamed sewage treatment plants water reclamation plants, called sewage used water, and opened the NEWater Visitor Centre

items.notes: Technology and public policy (Singapore). Reverse osmosis folded into ‘very fine filters’. The Malaysia supply background left out.

fixes: C reworded to narrow the length gap (key was 86 characters against 64 to 76)
review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: Wikipedia, NEWater: launched 2003; microfiltration, reverse osmosis, UV; anticipating safety concerns, PUB avoided “wastewater” and “sewage”, renamed plants water reclamation plants, opened a visitor centre.

items.passage: Thimlich Ohinga, in Kenya’s Migori County near Lake Victoria, is the largest of more than 130 archaeological sites in the region featuring stone enclosures. Its walls, which reach about four meters high in places, were constructed from rocks fitted tightly together without mortar, probably in the 1400s or earlier. According to oral traditions of the Luo people, who inhabit the area today, the enclosures were built to protect the communities inside them from wild animals, cattle raiders, and other enemies.
items.stem: According to the text, what do Luo oral traditions say about the enclosures?
options: They were built by the ancestors of the Luo people in the 1400s.
They were used mainly for storing food during the dry seasons.
They were the first stone structures ever built near Lake Victoria.
They were built to keep people safe from animals and attackers.
items.explanation: The text says that “according to oral traditions of the Luo people,” the enclosures “were built to protect the communities inside them from wild animals, cattle raiders, and other enemies.” Choice D restates this.

A.why_wrong: The 1400s date is given as a probable building date, not as part of the oral traditions, and the text never says who the builders were.

C.why_wrong: The text says Thimlich Ohinga is the largest of more than 130 such sites, not that the enclosures were the first stone structures in the region.

sources.what: Thimlich Ohinga, Migori County, Kenya: largest of 138 sites with 521 stone structures near Lake Victoria; walls 1 to 4.2 m high of stones set without mortar, densely packed and interlocking; believed to date to the 15th century or earlier; Luo oral traditions state the enclosures were built for protection against wild animals, cattle rustlers and other hostile groups; UNESCO World Heritage Site 2018

items.notes: Archaeology (Kenya). Builders’ identity left open, as the source leaves it.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: Wikipedia, Thimlich Ohinga: largest of 138 sites near Lake Victoria; walls up to about 4.5 m, no mortar; 15th century or earlier; Luo oral traditions say the enclosures protected against wild animals, cattle rustlers and enemies.

items.passage: Photographer Hugh Mangum (1877–1922) of Durham, North Carolina, spent years traveling by railroad throughout the South. He would establish a temporary tent studio for a few days at a time near railroad depots and circuses. At a time when segregation laws were spreading, he photographed both Black and white customers. Mangum kept no records of the individuals he photographed. But he did maintain a handwritten list of the towns he visited, first inside a suitcase and later inside the lid of a large trunk, and that list provides researchers with some of their best clues about where he worked.
items.stem: According to the text, what gives researchers clues about where Mangum worked?
options: Records he kept of the people he photographed
A handwritten list of the towns he visited
Advertisements he placed in local newspapers
Letters he sent to his family in Durham
items.explanation: Mangum maintained “a handwritten list of the towns he visited,” and “that list provides researchers with some of their best clues about where he worked.” Choice B names it.

A.why_wrong: “Mangum kept no records of the individuals he photographed.”

D.why_wrong: Durham is his hometown, but the text mentions no letters.

sources.what: Hugh Mangum (1877–1922), Durham, North Carolina, itinerant photographer: set up his studio tent near railroad depots and circuses, stayed one to seven days in a town; photographed Black and white sitters in the Jim Crow era; no records kept of the persons portrayed; handwritten log of towns begun inside a suitcase, later inside the lid of a large traveling trunk, gives some of the best clues to where he worked

items.notes: Arts and history (photography, US South). Options are noun phrases without a final period, as in official 1.4 and 1.9.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: Wikipedia, Hugh Mangum: tent studio near depots and circuses; Black and white sitters; no records of sitters; log of towns in a suitcase, later a trunk lid, gives the best clues to where he worked.

items.passage: Psychologists wanted to know whether small changes in what parents are told can affect how families behave at museum exhibits. At a gear exhibit in a children’s museum, researchers asked some parents to encourage their four- to six-year-old children to explain how the gears worked, asked others to encourage their children to explore, and gave a third group no special instructions. When parents had been told to encourage explaining, families talked more about how the gears worked. When parents had been told to encourage exploring, families spent more time connecting gears.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Psychologists think that children learn the most at museums when their parents give them no instructions at all.
Researchers found that children ages four to six are too young to explain how the gears in an exhibit work.
An experiment showed that children enjoy exhibits with gears more than other kinds of museum exhibits.
An experiment showed that simple instructions to parents can change how families engage with a museum exhibit.
items.explanation: Parents were given different instructions, and families behaved differently: those told to encourage explaining “talked more about how the gears worked,” and those told to encourage exploring “spent more time connecting gears.” Choice D sums up this finding.

A.why_wrong: The text compares the effects of different instructions; it never says the group without instructions learned the most.

B.why_wrong: Families told to encourage explaining talked more about how the gears worked, so the children were not shown to be too young to explain.

C.why_wrong: Only a gear exhibit is studied; the text never compares it with other exhibits.

sources.what: Willard, Busch, Cullum, Letourneau, Sobel, Callanan and Legare 2019, Child Development: parents at a children’s museum gear exhibit told to encourage their children (ages 4–6) to explain, explore, or engage as usual; encouragement to explain led to more discussion of gear mechanisms, encouragement to explore to more time connecting gears; minimal interventions shape parent-child interaction at an exhibit

items.notes: Social science (developmental psychology). Main idea spread over the method and the two results; no summary sentence states it.

fixes: opening sentence says “how families behave at museum exhibits” instead of “learn at museums” (the study measured interaction, not learning)
review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: PubMed abstract 30866040 (Willard et al. 2019): explain prompts led to more talk about gear mechanisms, explore prompts to more time connecting gears; minimal interventions shape parent-child interaction.

items.passage: Research on the sounds produced by marine fishes has traditionally concentrated on adults. But marine biologist Erica Staaterman and her team recorded the larvae of grey snappers, young fish that have not yet settled on a reef, both in the ocean and in a laboratory. The larvae produced “knock” and “growl” sounds at night, and these resembled the sounds made by adult snappers. The researchers suggest that the sounds may help the larvae remain together as a group in darkness, when visual signals are less effective.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers have found that young snappers make sounds that may help them stay in groups at night.
Adult snappers make knocking and growling sounds at night to warn their larvae of nearby danger.
Snapper larvae can hear sounds from much farther away than adult snappers can, especially in darkness.
Most marine fishes stop making sounds once they settle on a reef.
items.explanation: Staaterman’s team recorded grey snapper larvae producing “knock” and “growl” sounds at night and suggests that the sounds “may help the larvae remain together as a group in darkness.” Choice A states this finding with the researchers’ hedge.

B.why_wrong: The larvae made the sounds, which resembled adults’ sounds; nothing says adults warn larvae.

C.why_wrong: The text compares the sounds larvae and adults make, not how well they hear.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about fish falling silent after settling.

sources.what: Staaterman, Paris and Kough 2014, Biology Letters: acoustic ecology of marine fishes has focused on adults; first recordings of pre-settlement grey snapper (Lutjanus griseus) larvae, in situ and in the laboratory; larvae active at night producing knock and growl sounds similar to adults’; sounds may help larvae maintain group cohesion at night when visual cues are reduced

items.notes: Natural science (marine biology). Main idea in the last two sentences, hedge copied (may).

fixes: B and C lengthened so the key is not the longest option (key was 98 characters against 62 to 80)
review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: PubMed abstract 25274018 (Staaterman, Paris, Kough 2014): first recordings of pre-settlement grey snapper larvae; knock and growl sounds at night like adults’; may keep larvae together when visual cues are reduced.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Marshall Saunders’s 1893 novel Beautiful Joe. The narrator, a dog named Joe, has just arrived by train with his owner, Miss Laura, to visit her aunt and uncle, Mr. and Mrs. Wood, in the country.

It made me feel very welcome to have them both notice me, and I was so glad to be out of the train that I frisked for joy around their feet as we went to the wagon. I sat on the seat beside Mr. Wood, and sniffed in the delicious air, and the lovely smell of flowers and grass. How glad I was to be in the country! What long races I should have in the green fields. I wished that I had another dog to run with me, and wondered very much whether Mr. Wood kept one.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Joe is nervous about meeting a dog that Mr. Wood may keep on his farm.
Joe is still frightened by the train ride and wants to stay close to Miss Laura.
Joe is delighted to be in the country and looks forward to running in the fields.
Joe feels ignored by Miss Laura’s relatives and wishes he were back at home.
items.explanation: Joe “frisked for joy,” says “How glad I was to be in the country!” and imagines the “long races I should have in the green fields.” Choice C sums up his delight.

A.why_wrong: Joe wonders whether Mr. Wood keeps a dog because he wishes “that I had another dog to run with me,” not because he is nervous.

B.why_wrong: Joe is “so glad to be out of the train” and frisks for joy.

D.why_wrong: It “made me feel very welcome to have them both notice me.”

sources.what: text of Beautiful Joe (1893), chapter XVI, Dingley Farm; Mr. and Mrs. Wood are Miss Laura’s uncle and aunt

items.notes: Literature (Canadian novel, 1893, public domain). Adapted by cutting the paragraph about the horses and the wagon at sentence boundaries; wording otherwise exact.

review.facts_note: Excerpt checked against Gutenberg #2818, chapter XVI: exact, the horses passage cut at sentence boundaries.

items.passage: Clara Porset (1895–1981), a designer born in Cuba, moved to Mexico in 1935 and is considered a pioneer of furniture design there. Her modern furniture drew on traditional Mexican forms and materials. For example, she created updated versions of the butaque, a type of chair from Mexico’s colonial period, and she used woven fibers from the agave plant. In 1952 she organized an exhibition called Arte en la vida diaria (Art in Daily Life), which displayed well-designed objects made in Mexico for everyday use.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Porset was the first designer in Mexico to make furniture from the woven fibers of the agave plant.
Porset created modern furniture that was inspired by traditional Mexican designs and materials.
Porset preferred organizing exhibitions to designing furniture.
Porset’s furniture became less traditional after she organized her 1952 exhibition.
items.explanation: Porset’s “modern furniture drew on traditional Mexican forms and materials,” as her updated butaque chairs and her use of “woven fibers from the agave plant” show. Choice B states this main idea.

A.why_wrong: She used agave fibers, but the text never says she was the first designer in Mexico to do so.

C.why_wrong: The text mentions one exhibition she organized and says nothing about which work she preferred.

D.why_wrong: The text describes no change in her furniture after 1952.

sources.what: Clara Porset (1895–1981): Cuban-born furniture and interior designer, in Mexico from 1935, considered a pioneer of furniture design there; her furniture updated vernacular Mexican materials (woven agave fibers) and forms (the colonial butaque chair); in 1952 curated the exhibition Arte en la vida diaria of well-designed objects made in Mexico

items.notes: Arts (design, Mexico and Cuba). Profile with two examples and an exhibition.

fixes: A lengthened so the key is not the longest option (key was 95 characters against 63 to 83)
review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: Wikipedia, Clara Porset: Cuban-born, in Mexico from 1935, pioneer of Mexican modern design; updated the butaque and used woven agave fibers; 1952 exhibition Arte en la vida diaria.
